claims.text: Surface aluminization improves the high-temperature oxygen resistance of refractory high-entropy alloys.
The improvement results from formation of a continuous protective alumina scale.
Nb-containing refractory alloys can contain bcc solid solutions contaminated with oxygen.
As-cast or heat-treated refractory high-entropy alloys normally develop oxygen-contaminated regions upon high-temperature exposure.
Diffusion aluminization enriches the alloy's outer layer with aluminum.
The proposed benefit should occur during exposure to air at approximately 800°C for 100 hours.
Aluminization produces a dense, continuous Al2O3 scale on the alloy surface.
Surface-enriched aluminum reacts with oxygen to form a stable and adherent alumina scale.
The alumina scale acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
Limiting oxygen diffusion reduces oxidation-driven contamination of the underlying Nb-rich solid solution.
Relative to an untreated alloy, an aluminized sample should have a lower near-surface oxygen concentration after oxidation.
Relative to an untreated alloy, an aluminized sample should form fewer oxygen-contaminated phases.
Relative to an untreated alloy, an aluminized sample should retain hardness and Young's modulus better after oxidation.
Untreated Nb-containing refractory high-entropy alloys can exhibit oxygen contamination of Nb-based solid solutions.
Oxygen ingress into untreated refractory high-entropy alloys consequently degrades their mechanical properties.
The benefit of aluminization diminishes when the alumina scale is discontinuous.
Alloy compositions that do not support robust alumina-scale adhesion receive less benefit from aluminization.
Temperatures or exposure durations beyond the alumina layer's stability limits diminish the treatment's benefit.
The proposed aluminization mechanism is well supported in similar alloy systems.
